meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to say, to tell', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'hello, hey', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Алло, Танечка! В свои годы это нормально.
examples.trans: Hello, Tanechka! At my age that's normal.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лушать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to listen', paired with 'послушать'.

examples.text: Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
examples.trans: Listen, Samson, I've been thinking. Your boss is such an experienced specialist.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'дыхать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to rest, relax', paired with 'отдохнуть'.

examples.trans: Everything is great, get some rest!
In the summer we vacation by the sea.

examples.text: Всё отлично, отдыхай! Сегодня выходные, всё круто!
examples.trans: Everything is great, get some rest! It is the weekend today, everything is cool!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'покойно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Его не будет часа два. Вы спокойно всё сделаете.
examples.trans: He'll be gone for about two hours. You'll do everything calmly.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'uh-huh, yeah', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Yeah, right, like with the Cayenne?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'вязь'). Common feminine noun meaning 'connection, link' in everyday Russian.
Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('bad').

examples.text: Я вчера ел маринованные грибы. Может, один гриб был плохой.
examples.trans: Yesterday I ate pickled mushrooms. Maybe one mushroom was bad.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very, very much', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'mouse' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: A small mouse got caught in the mousetrap.

examples.text: Боже мой, это же мёртвая мышь!
examples.trans: My God, that is a dead mouse!
You destroyed a little defenseless mouse!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('small, fine, shallow, petty').

examples.trans: You don't read the small print.
There is only small change in my pocket.

examples.text: Женщина, вы мелкими буквами не читаете. Наша фирма в этом не виновата.
examples.trans: Ma'am, you don't read the small print. Our firm isn't to blame for that.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to wait, to expect', paired with 'подождать'.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'hall, large room; courtroom' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Understood. And who is managing the dining room?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

встать.gloss: to stand up, to get up

meanings.en: to stand up, to get up
meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'тать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to stand up, to get up', paired with 'вставать'.

examples.text: Кто первый встал, того и тапки.
examples.trans: First come, first served (whoever got up first gets the slippers).

examples.text: Юля, встала и пошла мыть посуду!
examples.trans: Yulia, get up and go wash the dishes!

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Лёва! Ты ещё здесь? Живо в архив!
examples.trans: Lyova! Are you still here? Off to the archive, now!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for; behind', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Common feminine noun meaning 'work, job' in everyday Russian.
High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes, indeed', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to give; (imperative) let's', paired with 'дать'.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'uniform, form, shape' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The cook put on a clean uniform.

examples.text: Шеф, мне не выдали форму вовремя.
examples.trans: Chef, they did not issue my uniform on time.
All employees wear a clean uniform.
